competency_fulfillment.rationale: The model each stem describes cannot exist. A shape is divided into 3 equal parts and 5 parts are shaded is a physical impossibility, as are the eight-part shape with 18 shaded and the two-part shape with 3 shaded. Fractions greater than one are represented with more than one whole, and by compressing them into a single shape the node teaches a false picture of exactly the idea it exists to introduce.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both categories the competency names are generated, with equal-to-one cases at 8/8, 5/5 and 6/6 and greater-than-one cases across a range of denominators, and the answers are left unreduced, which is correct when the point is representation rather than simplification.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Asking a third grader to accept that more parts are shaded than the shape contains creates a contradiction they cannot resolve, and it arrives at the very moment improper fractions are first met. The numeric demand itself, naming a fraction from a count of parts, is otherwise appropriate for this quarter.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Only two formatters appear and both deliver the same verbal description of a partitioned shape. For a competency whose wording ends in using models, no sample uses the shading or array-reading presentations that this generator demonstrably produces elsewhere, so the model itself is never actually put in front of the pupil.

competency_alignment.rationale: What varies across samples is the relationship between the shaded count and the number of parts, moving from exactly equal through moderately greater to more than triple, which is the correct progression for distinguishing fractions equal to one from those greater than one.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Denominators stay between 2 and 8 and numerators reach no higher than 18, keeping the fractions small enough to be modelled with two or three wholes, which is the right magnitude for a first encounter with improper fractions.
